html:
Sunken Face From Missing Teeth: Causes and Treatment Options

Understanding how tooth loss may contribute to changes in facial structure and what restorative options may help support oral function and appearance.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation020 71833573

Teeth play an important role in supporting the structure of the face, particularly the lower third. The roots of the teeth sit within the jawbone, and together they provide a framework that helps maintain the shape and proportions of the cheeks, lips, and jawline.

When teeth are lost, the underlying jawbone may gradually begin to change. Without the stimulation provided by the tooth roots, the bone can slowly reduce in volume over time. These structural changes can affect the appearance of the lower face, and some individuals notice a sunken or collapsed facial appearance after tooth loss.

The extent and speed of these changes varies between individuals and depends on several factors, including the number of teeth lost, how long they have been missing, and the patient's overall health. Professional dental assessment can help determine whether restorative options such as dental implants may help support oral function and facial structure.

How Missing Teeth Affect Facial Structure

Teeth help maintain the vertical height of the lower face. When the upper and lower teeth come together, they establish a relationship that supports the surrounding soft tissues — including the cheeks, lips, and the skin around the mouth. This interplay between teeth, bone, and soft tissue contributes to the natural proportions of the face.

The jawbone provides a structural foundation that supports these surrounding facial tissues. When teeth are present, the bone is maintained through the natural forces of chewing and biting. However, when teeth are lost, this support can gradually decrease as the bone begins to remodel.

Over time, the loss of bone and tooth structure may affect the cheeks, which can appear flatter or more hollow. The lips may lose some of their natural support, and the jawline can become less defined. These changes can contribute to an aged or sunken appearance in some individuals, although the extent varies considerably from person to person.

The Role of Jawbone Loss

The jawbone relies on regular stimulation from the roots of the teeth to maintain its density and volume. Each time the teeth are used for chewing or biting, small forces are transmitted through the roots into the surrounding bone. This mechanical stimulation signals the body to continue maintaining and renewing the bone tissue.

After tooth loss, this stimulation is no longer present in the affected area. Without these regular signals, the bone may gradually shrink through a natural process known as resorption. The rate of bone loss can be most significant in the first year following extraction, though it typically continues at a slower pace over subsequent years.

As bone volume reduces, the structural support for the overlying facial tissues is diminished. This can contribute to a sunken appearance around the mouth or cheeks, particularly when multiple teeth have been missing for an extended period. The degree of bone loss and its visible effect on facial appearance varies between individuals based on factors such as genetics, overall health, and the location and number of missing teeth.

Signs of Facial Changes After Tooth Loss

Facial changes following tooth loss tend to develop gradually over time and may not be immediately noticeable. However, certain signs may indicate that structural changes are occurring in the jaw and surrounding tissues:

A sunken or collapsed appearance around the mouth area
Reduced lip support, causing the lips to appear thinner or turned inward
Noticeable changes in the facial profile when viewed from the side
Increased wrinkling or creasing of the skin around the mouth
A reduced lower facial height, bringing the chin closer to the nose
Hollowing of the cheeks or a flattened appearance in the mid-face
Changes in the way dentures fit as the underlying bone shape alters
A prematurely aged appearance that may not reflect the patient’s actual age

These changes may occur gradually over months or years. If any of these signs are present, professional assessment can help determine the current state of the jawbone and whether treatment may be beneficial.

Treatment Options That May Help Restore Support

Several restorative dental treatments may help address the structural changes associated with tooth loss. The most appropriate option depends on the number of teeth missing, the condition of the remaining jawbone, and the patient's overall oral health. Treatment suitability is determined through detailed clinical evaluation.

Single Dental Implants

For individual missing teeth, a single tooth implant may help maintain bone in the affected area. The implant root provides stimulation to the jawbone, which may help support the surrounding facial tissues and prevent further bone loss at the implant site.

Multiple Dental Implants

When several teeth are missing, a multiple dental implant approach aims to restore oral function across a broader area. Replacing multiple teeth with implant-supported restorations may help support facial structure by maintaining bone volume in several areas of the jaw.

Full Arch Implant Bridge

For extensive tooth loss, a full arch implant bridge may help restore both function and structural support across an entire arch. This approach uses strategically placed implants to support a fixed bridge, which may help support facial structure and improve oral function.

Implant Retained Dentures

Implant retained dentures offer improved stability compared with conventional removable dentures. By securing the denture to dental implants, this option may provide better support for facial tissues and improve confidence when eating and speaking.

When Bone Augmentation May Be Recommended

In some cases, significant jawbone loss following tooth extraction may mean that there is insufficient bone volume to support dental implants without prior augmentation. When this occurs, bone augmentation procedures may be recommended as part of the overall treatment plan.

Bone grafting procedures involve placing bone or bone-substitute material into the area of deficiency to encourage new bone growth. This can help rebuild the jawbone to a volume that is sufficient to support implant placement. The grafting procedure typically requires a period of healing before implants can be placed.

In the upper jaw, a sinus lift procedure may be recommended where bone loss has occurred beneath the sinus cavities. This procedure creates additional space for bone grafting material, enabling implant placement in the posterior upper jaw where bone volume is commonly reduced after tooth loss.

The need for bone augmentation is assessed during the clinical evaluation and is based on detailed imaging and examination. Not all patients require these procedures, and the treatment plan is tailored to each individual's clinical needs.

Importance of Professional Implant Assessment

Implant treatment requires detailed clinical evaluation before a treatment plan can be developed. Each patient's situation is unique, and a thorough assessment helps ensure that any proposed treatment is appropriate and well-planned.

During the assessment, the clinician will evaluate the health and volume of the jawbone, the condition of the gum tissues, the overall bite function, and the patient's general medical history. Dental imaging — such as CBCT scans — may be used to provide a detailed three-dimensional view of the bone and surrounding structures.

Treatment planning varies between patients depending on the extent of tooth loss, the degree of bone resorption, and any other clinical factors. Professional guidance helps determine the most appropriate restorative options and ensures that the patient understands the treatment process, potential outcomes, and any associated risks.

Assessment and treatment planning for tooth loss and structural changes in the jaw are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options.
